newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss welcome British push for Nazi gold talks.
newsitem.headline: Swiss welcome British push for Nazi gold talks.

text.p: Switzerland on Tuesday welcomed an offer by Britain's new Labour government to host an international conference focusing on millions of dollars of gold seized by the Nazis during World War Two.

Switzerland has been at the centre of recent international interest in the fate of gold stolen by the Nazis, who sold much of their own stock and looted gold to the neutral Alpine republic and through it to other nations during World War Two.
A government spokeswoman said Switzerland welcomed the British idea in principle but could not comment further until it hears details of the idea proposed by new Foreign Secretary Robin Cook.

"We welcome an initiative like this but have to wait to hear directly from the British government," said Marie-Marceline Kurmann, spokeswoman for the Foreign Ministry's task force on Holocaust issues.

Kurmann said Berne had not been contacted since Cook earlier on Tuesday said there could be a strong case for compensating victims of Nazi persecution or their direct descendants for gold seized by Hitler's forces during World War Two.
Some critics have called on Switzerland to renegotiate a 1946 deal with the Allies on reparation payments for buying Nazi gold.
Berne has rejected those calls, arguing that the treaty with the United States, Britain and France settled for all time Allied claims against the Swiss for Nazi gold purchases.
Kurmann said this remained the government's stance. "Our position has not changed," she said.

Under the 1946 Washington accord, the Swiss paid 250 million Swiss francs (about $60 million at 1940s exchange rates) in return for the central bank buying Nazi gold totalling 1.2 billion Swiss francs at the time.
Gold worth another 400 million Swiss francs at then-prices passed through Switzerland from Hitler's Reichsbank to other countries and private Swiss banks.

The Swiss National Bank, which handled the gold transactions, has acknowledged that its wartime directors should have been more suspicious of the metal's origins based on reports the Nazis were looting the central banks of occupied countries.
But the central bank has said it never had any reason to suspect Nazi German gold might have come from Holocaust victims such as Jews in death camps whose teeth fillings and jewelry were melted down.
